unit.title: Your trading plan
unit.description: Write your plan, keep a journal, ride out the streaks and make the leap sensibly

steps.title: The parts of a plan
steps.body:
1. **Capital:** how much you set aside (a small % of your wealth).
2. **Markets and timeframe:** what you trade and on which chart.
3. **Entry:** specific, testable rules.
4. **Stop:** where and why.
5. **Size:** 1 % risk per trade.
6. **Exit:** target and time-based exit.
7. **What you don't do.**
8. **Limits:** when you stop.
9. **Review:** every 20 trades.

steps.title: Specific rules, not wishes
steps.body:
«I'll get in when it looks clear» isn't a rule. This is:

• «Price above the 200-session moving average, pullback to a support and a reversal candle with above-average volume.»
• «Stop below the low of the reversal candle, at least 1.5 ATR away.»
• «Half off at 2R; the rest with a stop below the latest higher low. If it hasn't reached 1R within 15 sessions, I get out.»

steps.title: Limits protect you from yourself
steps.body: «I don't trade on earnings day. I don't average down. I don't move the stop against me. If I lose 6 % in a month, I stop until the next month. If the account falls 15 % from its peak, I halve my risk and review the plan.»
steps.key: If it isn't written down, it isn't a plan: it's a hunch.
steps.tip: Write the plan when you're calm. You'll need it when you're not.

steps.title: What to write down
steps.body:
For each trade:

• Date, asset and direction.
• Reason for entry according to the plan.
• Entry, stop, target and what 1R is worth.
• Size.
• Result in € and in R.
• Did you follow the plan? If not, why?
• How you felt going in and coming out.
• A screenshot of the chart.

steps.title: What you get from the journal
steps.body:
• Win rate.
• Average win and loss in R.
• **Expectancy** per trade.
• Longest losing streak and maximum drawdown.
• Results of trades **within** the plan versus those that broke it (usually an eye-opener).

steps.title: Key takeaway
steps.body: Example entry: 12/11, buy at €4.10, stop €3.95, target €4.40, 1R = €100, 666 shares. Result: +€180, +1.8R. Followed the plan: yes. Feeling: calm.
steps.key: The journal turns your trades into data you can improve with.
steps.tip: Your journal shows you the mistakes your memory would rather forget.

steps.title: Streaks are normal
steps.body:
Simulating 20,000 sequences of 100 trades:

• With a **50 %** win rate, the typical longest losing streak is **6 in a row**.
• With **40 %** (like a profitable system that wins 2R), it's **7**, and almost half the time there are streaks of **8 or more**.

steps.title: Drawdown
steps.body:
It's the fall in the account from its peak to the next low. At 1 % risk, 8 losses in a row are −7.7 %. At 5 %, −33.7 %.

Rule in the example plan: if the account falls 10–15 % from its peak, you **halve your risk** and review.

steps.title: What a drawdown costs
steps.body: Set a 15 % fall and see how much you need to gain to get back to the peak. Then try 35 %.

steps.title: Key takeaway
steps.body: Eight losses in a row with a winning system don't mean it has stopped working. If you switch systems after every bad streak, you'll never know whether any of them worked.
steps.key: Streaks are statistics: risk little so you can get through them.
steps.tip: Eight misses in a row don't mean the plan is wrong: they mean you're in a streak.

u26l4.title: From the simulator to real money

steps.title: The four phases
steps.body:
1. **Backtest:** go back through the chart and record 50–100 signals with their results.
2. **Out-of-sample:** other assets or another period, **without changing the rules**.
3. **Real-time simulator:** 2–3 months at least.
4. **Real money, bit by bit:** a fraction of your capital and half the risk. You only scale up if the stats look similar.

steps.title: The traps
steps.body:
• **Over-optimising:** tweaking parameters until the past looks perfect.
• **Small sample:** with fewer than 30–50 trades, the stats mean almost nothing.
• **Survivorship:** testing only on companies that exist today.
• **Forgetting costs** and slippage.
• **Hindsight:** in the past everything «looks» clear.

steps.title: When to call it a day
steps.body: If after 100 well-logged trades your expectancy after costs is negative or close to zero, you don't have an edge. It's not a failure: it's information. Investing for the long term in a diversified portfolio is still the option with the best odds.
steps.key: A system isn't proven until it works on new data and with enough trades.
steps.tip: In the simulator you learn to trade. With real money you learn who you are. Start small.

s8boss.title: Final challenge: Risk, strategies and trading

u26l1-1.prompt: Put the parts of a trading plan in order.
u26l1-1.explanation: From the general (how much and what) to the specific (when I enter, how much I risk and how I exit).

u26l1-3.prompt: Monthly limit in the example plan: if I lose ____ in a month, I stop until the next month.
u26l1-3.explanation: A monthly cap cuts off revenge-trading spirals.

u26l1-4.prompt: Is it a specific rule or a vague phrase?
options: If it hasn't reached 1R within 15 sessions, I get out
I get out when it feels like enough
Stop below the low of the reversal candle, at least 1.5 ATR away
I enter if it bounces off the 50-session moving average with a reversal candle and above-average volume
I'll get in when it looks clear
u26l1-4.explanation: A specific rule can be checked: two people reading it would do the same thing.

u26l1-5.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: That's a wish; a plan says when you enter, where the stop is and how much you risk
You don't need a plan if you've got intuition
u26l1-5.explanation: A plan is a set of testable rules, not good intentions.
feedback: That's the problem: it doesn't say when I enter, where the stop is or how much I risk.
OK… Entry at a support with a reversal candle, stop below the low, 1 % risk and exit at 2R. Better?
Intuition can't be reviewed or improved. A written plan can.

u26l1-6.prompt: Which things go in the «What I don't do» section of the example plan? Select all that apply.
options: I don't move the stop against me
I don't trade on earnings day
u26l1-6.explanation: Not setting a stop would mean skipping the foundation of the plan.

u26l1-7.prompt: Your plan caps total open risk at 5 % of the account and each trade risks 1 %. What's the maximum number of trades you can have open at once?

u26l1-8.prompt: A good trading plan includes a prediction of what the market will do.
u26l1-8.explanation: A plan is a set of rules for acting whatever happens, not predictions.

u26l1-9.prompt: Pablo's plan says «I only enter on a reversal candle at a support». Today he sees a share shoot up 8 % in an hour that doesn't meet any of his rules. What does he do?
options: Gets in with double the size to make the most of it
Gets in: it's a once-in-a-lifetime chance
Doesn't get in and logs it in the journal as a temptation
u26l1-9.explanation: A plan only works if you follow it even when you don't feel like it.
feedback: Breaking the plan and doubling the risk too: two mistakes in one.
That «once-in-a-lifetime chance» is FOMO. If it goes wrong, he won't know whether his plan works or not.
Good: he sticks to the plan and learns from what he feels. There'll be plenty of chances.

u26l1-10.prompt: Your plan says: «stop below the recent low». Apply it to this buy on a real chart.
u26l1-10.explanation: A specific rule applies the same way on any chart: the stop goes just below the recent low.

u26l1-11.prompt: How often does the example plan suggest reviewing the stats?
u26l1-11.explanation: A single trade tells you nothing; 20 start to show you something.

u26l2-1.prompt: Match each journal field with an example.
u26l2-1.explanation: Each field answers a question that will later help you improve.
right: No: I went in without a signal
Bounce off the 50 average with a hammer

u26l2-2.prompt: Match each journal statistic with what it tells you.
u26l2-2.explanation: No single statistic tells the whole story.
right: Whether the system makes money in the long run
Whether breaking the rules costs you money
How much you have to sit through

u26l2-3.prompt: Risk per trade: €100. You enter at €4.10 with the stop at €3.95. How many shares do you buy? (round down)

u26l2-4.prompt: Your journal has 20 trades: 8 winners and 12 losers. What's your win rate?

u26l2-5.prompt: In those 20 trades, the winners made +2R on average and the losers −1R. What's your expectancy per trade?

u26l2-6.prompt: Which journal statistic tells you whether your system makes money in the long run?
u26l2-6.explanation: It combines your win rate with your average win and loss.

u26l2-7.prompt: After 40 trades, Marta's journal shows that the trades that followed the plan average +0.3R and those that broke it, −0.6R. What does she do?
options: Nothing, the numbers don't really matter
Focuses on not breaking the plan
u26l2-7.explanation: Comparing within and outside the plan is usually the most revealing part of the journal.
feedback: Her system makes money when she follows it. Changing it would throw away what works.
The numbers are telling her exactly where she's losing money.
Good: the problem isn't the system, it's the exceptions. That's where she can improve.

u26l2-8.prompt: To know how you're doing, your memory is as reliable as a journal.
u26l2-8.explanation: Memory remembers the wins and forgets the mistakes: the journal doesn't.

u26l2-9.prompt: Quick one: which journal column helps you spot FOMO?
u26l2-9.explanation: If you write down «rushed» or «afraid of missing out» when going in, you know what to look for.

u26l2-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Without a journal you can't work out your expectancy or see your mistakes
u26l2-10.explanation: What you don't measure, you can't improve.
feedback: Then your journal would say you're a genius… and it would ruin you.
Your memory keeps the trade that went brilliantly and forgets the five small losses.
OK… If in 20 trades I find out I lose when I trade in a rush, it's worth it.
lines: Keeping a journal is such a drag 😩
Anyway, I can remember my trades.

u26l3-1.prompt: With a system that's right 50 % of the time, is it unusual to have 6 losses in a row in 100 trades?
options: It only happens with bad systems
u26l3-1.explanation: It's the typical longest streak in 100 trades.

u26l3-2.prompt: You risk 1 % per trade and take 8 losses in a row. How much does your account fall? (round to one decimal place)

u26l3-3.prompt: Now risking 5 % per trade: 8 losses in a row. How much does the account fall? (round to one decimal place)
u26l3-3.explanation: 0.95⁸ ≈ 0.663 → a 33.7 % fall. The same streak, four times the damage.

u26l3-4.prompt: Match the risk per trade with the fall after 8 losses in a row.
u26l3-4.explanation: Fall = 1 − (1 − risk)⁸. At 10 %, a normal streak takes more than half.

u26l3-5.prompt: Your account falls 15 % from its peak. How much do you need to gain to get back to it? (round to one decimal place)

u26l3-6.prompt: Laura has 120 logged trades with positive expectancy. Now she's had 7 losses in a row. What does she do?
options: Sticks to her plan with the same risk and checks she's applying the rules properly
Doubles her risk to recover sooner
Switches systems: this one doesn't work any more
u26l3-6.explanation: A streak within what's expected is no reason to abandon a system with lots of trades behind it.
feedback: Good: she checks she hasn't skipped anything and lets the statistics do their job.
If the streak continues, the hole gets much deeper.
With a 40 % win rate, 7 in a row is the typical streak. Switching now means throwing away a system that works.

u26l3-7.prompt: Bruno's account falls 15 % from its peak. What does the example plan say?
options: Halve the risk and review the plan
u26l3-7.explanation: When the account falls, you protect first; then you analyse.
feedback: It's the most common reaction and the most dangerous.
Without stops, the fall could be much bigger.
That way he protects his capital while he works out what's going on.

u26l3-8.prompt: Eight losses in a row prove a system has stopped working.
u26l3-8.explanation: With a 40 % win rate, almost half the time there are streaks of 8 or more in 100 trades.

u26l3-9.prompt: Quick one: with a 40 % win rate, what's the typical losing streak in 100 trades?
u26l3-9.explanation: And almost half the time, 8 or more.

u26l3-10.prompt: The fall in the account from its peak to the next low is called ____.
u26l3-10.explanation: It's the measure that best reflects how much a strategy really hurts.

u26l4-1.prompt: Put the phases for validating a system in order.
u26l4-1.explanation: Each phase removes a type of self-deception before you risk money.

u26l4-2.prompt: If you win 12 of your first 15 trades, your system is proven.
u26l4-2.explanation: Fifteen trades is far too small a sample: it could be luck.

u26l4-3.prompt: Tweaking parameters until the past looks perfect improves future results.
u26l4-3.explanation: That's over-optimising: the system adapts to the noise of the past and usually fails afterwards.

u26l4-4.prompt: Raúl has won 12 of his first 15 trades and wants to move up to risking 10 % per trade «because his system works». What would you tell him?
options: Stick with 1 % and log 50–100 trades before drawing conclusions
Go for it, the numbers speak for themselves
Use leverage to make the most of the streak
u26l4-4.explanation: Small sample + high risk is the most dangerous combination.
feedback: Good: with a bigger sample and his expectancy worked out after costs, he'll know whether he has an edge.
At 10 %, a normal streak of 6–8 losses would cost him between half and two thirds of the account.
Good streaks end; leverage would make the bad one take him out of the game.

u26l4-5.prompt: Marta has passed the first three phases and is going to use real money. How does she start?
options: With all the capital she planned and the same risk as in the simulator
With double the risk to make up for lost time
With a small fraction of her capital and half the risk per trade
u26l4-5.explanation: The move to real money is made in small steps and only scaled up with data.
feedback: Real emotions are different: better to discover them with little money at stake.
There's no lost time: there's impatience, and impatience is a bad adviser.
Good: if her real stats look like the simulator's, she scales up bit by bit.

u26l4-6.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Better with a loan, so you make more
First more logged trades; then a small part and half the risk
u26l4-6.explanation: A good month on the simulator is a starting point, not proof.
feedback: With debt, a bad streak can be a serious problem.
OK: 100 trades in the journal, expectancy after costs and start small.
A month is very little… and with real money, fear and impatience change how I trade.
lines: I made 20 % on the simulator this month 🏆
Can I put my savings in now?

u26l4-7.prompt: Match each statistical trap with its description.
u26l4-7.explanation: They all make a system look better than it is.
right: Testing only on companies that still exist
Seeing a signal in the past as crystal clear when it wasn't in real time
Tweaking parameters until the past looks perfect

u26l4-8.prompt: With real money, emotions usually weigh more than in the simulator.
u26l4-8.explanation: That's why you start small: to find out how you really react.

u26l4-9.prompt: You're going to start with €2,000 of real money and half your usual 1 % risk. How much do you risk per trade?

u26l4-10.prompt: First «small» trade: your account is €2,000 and, since you're just starting, you risk 0.5 % at most. Choose the stop and amount.
u26l4-10.explanation: With half your usual risk, a bad streak when you start with real money won't take you out of the game while you check whether your stats look like the simulator's.

u26l4-11.prompt: What changes when you move from the simulator to real money? Select all that apply.
options: Your emotions when you see real losses
u26l4-11.explanation: The maths is the same; what changes is how you react, real costs and the taxman.
